claim: Working memory has limited capacity.
source: A well-known feature of working memory (WM) is its limited capacity (Baddeley, 2000; Cowan, 2001), which constrains the amount of information that can be temporarily retained for future behavior.
evidence: Supported by citations to Baddeley, 2000 and Cowan, 2001

claim: Memorized items in daily experiences share common frameworks or structures that can be leveraged to compress information and overcome working memory capacity limitations.
source: Meanwhile, in daily experiences, memorized items do not exist independently but are always part of a common framework or share the same structure, which could be leveraged to compress information and overcome the WM capacity challenge (Brady et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brady et al., 2011

claim: Items at a supermarket can be grouped into categories such as drinks, vegetables, fruits, and meats to facilitate memory.
source: For example, while shopping at a supermarket, numerous items could be grouped into a few categories, such as drinks, vegetables, fruits, and meats, to facilitate memory.
evidence: This is presented as an example of how common frameworks facilitate memory, drawing on general knowledge about categorization

claim: Abstract associations such as relational regularities and structure schema can mediate working memory organization.
source: Other types of abstract associations such as relational regularities and structure schema could also mediate WM organization (Al Roumi et al., 2021; Gathercole and Baddeley, 2014; Mathy and Feldman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Al Roumi et al., 2021; Gathercole and Baddeley, 2014; Mathy and Feldman, 2012

claim: Higher-order structures such as summaries and relative relations reduce memory uncertainty by constraining individual-item representations.
source: Computational modeling also suggests that higher-order structures (e.g. summaries and relative relations) would reduce memory uncertainty by constraining individual-item representations (Brady and Tenenbaum, 2013; Ding et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to computational modeling studies by Brady and Tenenbaum, 2013 and Ding et al., 2017

claim: Cognitive maps are a type of spatial schema.
source: Cognitive maps, as one type of spatial schema (Farzanfar et al., 2023; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017), provide a general structure framework for organizing information in different tasks and across various domains (Tolman, 1948; Whittington et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Farzanfar et al., 2023 and Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017

claim: Cognitive maps provide a general structure framework for organizing information in different tasks and across various domains.
source: Cognitive maps, as one type of spatial schema (Farzanfar et al., 2023; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017), provide a general structure framework for organizing information in different tasks and across various domains (Tolman, 1948; Whittington et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tolman, 1948 and Whittington et al., 2020

claim: Cognitive maps were first identified as representations of physical maps during navigation.
source: They were first identified as representations of physical maps during navigation, but recently have been shown to also support other higher-level processes, such as conceptual knowledge, reasoning, planning, and decision-making (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is a historical statement about cognitive maps supported by citations

claim: Cognitive maps support higher-level processes such as conceptual knowledge, reasoning, planning, and decision-making.
source: They were first identified as representations of physical maps during navigation, but recently have been shown to also support other higher-level processes, such as conceptual knowledge, reasoning, planning, and decision-making (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978

claim: Grid-like code is a major neural signature of cognitive maps.
source: Two major neural signatures of cognitive maps, grid-like code (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Doeller et al., 2010; Hafting et al., 2005; Park et al., 2021), and neural replay in the hippocampal-entorhinal system (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996), are identified in both spatial and non-spatial tasks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Constantinescu et al., 2016; Doeller et al., 2010; Hafting et al., 2005; Park et al., 2021

claim: Neural replay in the hippocampal-entorhinal system is a major neural signature of cognitive maps.
source: Two major neural signatures of cognitive maps, grid-like code (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Doeller et al., 2010; Hafting et al., 2005; Park et al., 2021), and neural replay in the hippocampal-entorhinal system (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996), are identified in both spatial and non-spatial tasks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster and Wilson, 2006; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996

claim: Grid-like code and neural replay are identified in both spatial and non-spatial tasks.
source: Two major neural signatures of cognitive maps, grid-like code (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Doeller et al., 2010; Hafting et al., 2005; Park et al., 2021), and neural replay in the hippocampal-entorhinal system (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996), are identified in both spatial and non-spatial tasks.
evidence: Supported by the combined citations for both grid-like code and neural replay

claim: Neural replay is the rapid item-by-item reactivation in a forward or backward direction.
source: Neural replay, the rapid item-by-item reactivation in a forward or backward direction, is posited to not only repeat past experiences, but also reflect an internal model of the world (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2023; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations

claim: Neural replay is posited to not only repeat past experiences but also reflect an internal model of the world.
source: Neural replay, the rapid item-by-item reactivation in a forward or backward direction, is posited to not only repeat past experiences, but also reflect an internal model of the world (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2023; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kurth-Nelson et al., 2023 and Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018

claim: Many higher-level processes can be described as mental explorations of a sequence of states within an abstract map, similar to tracing a route on a physical map.
source: Accordingly, many higher-level processes could be described as mental explorations of a sequence of states within an abstract map, similar to tracing a route on a physical map.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous discussion about cognitive maps

claim: A cognitive map can serve as a common reference for aligning different features or domains.
source: As a result, a cognitive map can serve as a common reference for aligning different features or domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of cognitive maps as general frameworks

claim: Conjoined cognitive maps have been revealed in the rodent hippocampus for physical space and abstract task variables.
source: In line with the view, conjoined cognitive maps have been recently revealed in the rodent hippocampus (i.e. physical space and abstract task variables) (Nieh et al., 2021), and alignment of different feature maps speeds learning performance (Aho et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nieh et al., 2021

claim: Alignment of different feature maps speeds learning performance.
source: In line with the view, conjoined cognitive maps have been recently revealed in the rodent hippocampus (i.e. physical space and abstract task variables) (Nieh et al., 2021), and alignment of different feature maps speeds learning performance (Aho et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aho et al., 2022

claim: Both spatial and conceptual distances are relied on to generalize when searching for correlated rewards in value-guided learning.
source: Moreover, both spatial and conceptual distances are relied on to generalize when searching for correlated rewards in value-guided learning, supporting a cognitive-map-dependent computational mechanism (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020

claim: Cognitive maps might be employed to reorganize memory information across domains to overcome capacity bottlenecks in working memory.
source: Based on these findings, we hypothesize that cognitive maps might be employed to reorganize memory information across domains to overcome capacity bottlenecks in WM.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on prior literature

claim: Thirty-three human participants performed a visual sequence working memory task while their brain activities were recorded using EEG.
source: Thirty-three human participants performed a visual sequence WM task while their brain activities were recorded using EEG.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure conducted by the authors

claim: Participants were required to memorize a color sequence presented at a list of spatial locations and later reproduce both the color and location sequences on two rings.
source: Here, we examined whether cognitive maps shared by multiple feature domains would be naturally leveraged to make efficient use of limited WM capacity. To address this question, participants were asked to memorize a color sequence presented at a list of spatial locations and later reproduce both the color and location sequences on two rings, one after another.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design

claim: In the aligned condition, the color and location sequences share a common spatial trajectory with the same distance between successive items between maps.
source: Specifically, for the aligned condition, the color and location sequence share a common spatial trajectory, i.e., separated by the same distance between successive items between maps (Figure 1B), whereas, for the misaligned condition, they have distinct relative trajectories (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1B

claim: In the misaligned condition, color and location sequences have distinct relative trajectories.
source: Specifically, for the aligned condition, the color and location sequence share a common spatial trajectory, i.e., separated by the same distance between successive items between maps (Figure 1B), whereas, for the misaligned condition, they have distinct relative trajectories (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1C

claim: Sequences with consistent color-location trajectories (aligned condition) show enhanced memory precision compared to misaligned condition.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, two-way repeated ANOVA (alignment (AT vs. MAT)×task (location vs. color)) revealed significant main effects for alignment (F(1,32) = 4.279, p=0.047, ηp2 = 0.118) and task (F(1,32) = 139.382, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.813), but nonsignificant interaction effect (F(1,32) = 0.618, p=0.438, ηp2 = 0.019).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The aligned trajectory condition had better memory performance than the misaligned trajectory condition.
source: Specifically, the AT condition had better memory performance than the MAT condition, supporting our hypothesis that shared structure facilitates memory of multiple sequences.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the statistical results from the behavioral data

claim: Location memory performed better than color memory.
source: Moreover, location memory performed better than color memory.
evidence: This is based on the main effect of task from the ANOVA results

claim: The aligned condition mainly enhanced color memory but not location memory.
source: Further comparison revealed that the aligned condition mainly enhanced color memory (paired-t test, t(32) = 2.446, p=0.020, Cohen's d=0.426) but not location (paired-t test, t(32) = 1.538, p=0.134, Cohen's d=0.268).
evidence: Supported by paired t-test statistical results

claim: Color sequences demonstrated better memory performance under aligned versus misaligned conditions, especially for the second and third items.
source: In terms of serial position in sequence, color sequences demonstrated better memory performance under AT versus MAT conditions, especially for the second and third items (paired-t test, first: t(32) = –0.315, p=0.755, Cohen's d=0.055; second: t(32) = 4.069, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.709; third: t(32) = 2.583, p=0.015, Cohen's d=0.450) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by paired t-test statistical results and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Location sequences exhibited similar performance for all positions between aligned and misaligned conditions.
source: Meanwhile, the location sequences exhibited similar performance for all positions (paired-t test, first: t(32) = 0.972, p=0.338, Cohen's d=0.169; second: t(32) = 1.245, p=0.222, Cohen's d=0.216; third: t(32) = 1.290, p=0.206, Cohen's d=0.225) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by paired t-test statistical results showing no significant differences, and shown in Figure 2C

claim: The aligned trajectory condition showed significant correlations for both first-second and second-third trajectories in recalled location and color trajectory errors.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, the AT condition showed significant correlations for both first-second (one-sample t-test, t (32)=5.022, p<0.001) and second-third (one-sample t-test, t (32)=3.113, p=0.004) trajectories, but not for first- third trajectory (one-sample t-test, t (32)=1.579, p=0.124).
evidence: Supported by one-sample t-test statistical results and shown in Figure 2D

claim: The misaligned trajectory condition did not display any significant correlation in trajectory errors between location and color.
source: In contrast, the MAT condition did not display any significant correlation (one-sample t-test; first- second: t (32)=1.361, p=0.183; second-third: t (32)=0.490, p=0.628; first-third: t (32)=–0.582, p=0.565).
evidence: Supported by one-sample t-test statistical results showing no significant correlations

claim: At the group level, a significant correlation was observed for the first-second and second-third trajectory in the aligned condition.
source: As shown in Figure 2 EFG, a significant correlation was observed for the first-second (r=0.270, p=0.002) and second-third trajectory (r=0.279, p=0.002), but not for the first-third trajectory (r=0.077, p=0.375).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 2E, 2F, and 2G

claim: The location of each of the three disks could be successfully decoded from EEG signals for both aligned and misaligned conditions during stimulus presentation period.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the location of each of the three disks could be successfully decoded from EEG signals for both AT (first location: 0.03–0.56 s, 1.14–1.26 s, 1.55–1.84 s; second location: 1.56–2.10 s, 2.65–2.92 s, 3.12–3.35 s; third location: 3.06–3.50 s; corrected cluster p<0.001) and MAT conditions (first location: 0.03–0.52 s, 1.15–1.39 s, 1.58–1.84 s,; second location: 1.52–2.10 s, 3.11–3.36 s; third location: 3.06–3.54 s; corrected cluster p<0.001) during stimulus presentation period.
evidence: Supported by neural decoding analysis with cluster-based permutation test shown in Figure 3A

claim: Color information could be decoded from EEG signals for both aligned and misaligned conditions during stimulus presentation period.
source: Similarly, color information could also be decoded for both AT (first color: 0.09–0.50 s, corrected cluster p<0.001;second color: 1.57–2.01 s, corrected cluster p<0.001; third color: 3.11–3.49 s, corrected cluster p=0.002) and MAT conditions (first color: 0.04–0.45 s; second color: 1.57–1.91 s, corrected cluster p<0.001; third color: 3.11–3.55 s; corrected cluster p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by neural decoding analysis with cluster-based permutation test shown in Figure 3B

claim: The color feature exhibited weaker decoding strength than location.
source: It is noteworthy that location and color features were generated with the constraint that they could not occupy the same position within their respective rings. This thereby ensured the independent decoding of location and color features from the same neural signals. Moreover, the color feature exhibited weaker decoding strength than location, also consistent with behavioral results (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed from the neural decoding results and is consistent with behavioral findings

claim: During the 'recall location' period, the currently task-relevant location sequence displayed strong decoding performance for the first location and weak but significant decoding performance for the third location, but not for the second location, in the aligned trajectory condition.
source: As shown in Figure 4A (left panel), the currently task-relevant location sequence during AT condition displayed strong decoding performance for the first location (0.11–0.46 s, corrected cluster p=0.003), weak but significant decoding performance for the third location (0.27–0.41 s, corrected cluster p=0.011), but not for the second location.
evidence: Supported by neural decoding analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: The aligned trajectory condition showed significant reactivation of color sequence during the 'recall location' period.
source: As shown in the left panel of Figure 4B, we observed significant reactivation of color sequence for the AT condition. Specifically, the color sequence undergoes a temporally compressed, forward reply (first color: 0.10–0.16 s, corrected cluster p=0.048; second color: 0.21–0.27 s, corrected cluster p=0.046; third color: 0.31–0.38 s, corrected cluster p=0.089).
evidence: Supported by neural decoding analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The misaligned trajectory condition did not display any neural reactivation of the color sequence during the 'recall location' period.
source: In contrast, the MAT condition did not display any neural reactivation of the color sequence (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by neural decoding analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Direct comparison between aligned and misaligned conditions showed a significant reactivation difference.
source: Direct comparison between AT and MAT conditions showed a significant reactivation difference (two-way repeated ANOVA, F(1,32) = 14.213, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.308).
evidence: Supported by two-way repeated ANOVA statistical analysis

claim: The aligned-misaligned difference in color reactivation is mainly due to the first and second items.
source: Further analysis (Figure 4C) reveals that the AT-MAT difference is mainly due to the first (paired test, t(32) = 3.151, p=0.004, Cohen's d=0.548) and second items (t(32) = 1.914, p=0.065, Cohen's d=0.334).
evidence: Supported by paired t-test statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Color sequence replay showed a significant temporal lag around 110 ms and 140 ms for the first-second and second-third color pairs, respectively, indicating a forward replay profile with temporal compression within approximately 130 ms.
source: Figure 4D shows a significant temporal lag around 110 ms and 140 ms for the first-second and second-third color pairs, respectively, indicating a forward replay profile with temporal compression within approximately 130 ms (peak of the average of the two cross-correlation time courses).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: A significant correlation was found between the empirical cross-correlation matrix and the theoretical forward transition pattern at 130 ms time lag.
source: A significant correlation was found between the empirical cross-correlation matrix and the theoretical transitional pattern (r=0.690, p=0.040), further confirming the forward replay of the color sequence.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between theoretical and empirical patterns shown in Figure 4E

claim: The first-to-second trajectory appeared right after the presentation of the second item for the aligned trajectory condition during encoding.
source: During the encoding period (Figure 5A), the first-to-second trajectory appeared right after the presentation of the second item for AT condition (1.55–2.11 s, corrected cluster p<0.001), which is expected since the relationship between the first and second items along the trajectory can only be established when the second item occurs.
evidence: Supported by trajectory decoding analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The second-to-third trajectory appeared after onset of the third item during encoding in the aligned trajectory condition.
source: Similarly, the second-to-third trajectory appeared after onset of the third item (3.10–3.48 s, corrected cluster p<0.001) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by trajectory decoding analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The first-third trajectory showed nonsignificant neural decoding during encoding.
source: In contrast, the first-third trajectory showed nonsignificant neural decoding (Figure 5C), consistent with the nonsignificant color-location trajectory correlation in behavior.
evidence: Supported by trajectory decoding analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: The first-to-second trajectory was reactivated right after the third item during encoding in the aligned trajectory condition.
source: Most interestingly, the first-to-second trajectory was reactivated right after the third item (3.19–3.48 s, corrected cluster p=0.006; Figure 5A), implicating the formed link between the two trajectories (first-second and second-third) for aligned location-color sequences.
evidence: Supported by trajectory decoding analysis showing reactivation in Figure 5A

claim: Only the higher-correlation group exhibited a significant reactivation of the first-to-second trajectory after the onset of the third item.
source: Meanwhile, only the higher-correlation group exhibited a significant reactivation of the first-to-second trajectory after the onset of the third item (3.25–3.46 s, corrected cluster p=0.018, 3.55–3.68 s, corrected cluster p=0.088; Higher group vs. Lower group: bootstrap test, p=0.037, two-side).
evidence: Supported by trajectory decoding analysis comparing high and low correlation groups shown in Figure 5D

claim: Higher trajectory representation group was accompanied with clearer forward replay.
source: Moreover, we were curious about the correlation between the common trajectory representation and latter forward replay pattern. Therefore, based on the average of trajectory neural representation (first-second and second-third trajectories) during presentation of the third item when common trajectory reactivation was observed, we divided all participants into two groups, and observed higher trajectory representation group was accompanied with clearer forward replay (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The aligned condition showed significant and long-lasting decoding of compression trajectories during the retention period based on alpha-band activities.
source: With regards to the retention period, based on previous literatures (de Vries et al., 2020; Foster et al., 2016; Fukuda et al., 2016; Sutterer et al., 2019), we chose to rely on the alpha-band activities to decode shared trajectories (see decoding results based on raw signals in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B). The aligned condition showed significant and long-lasting decoding of compression trajectories (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D), while the misaligned condition only showed decoding at the beginning, which might be due to the non- offset response of the third item (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Supported by alpha-band decoding analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Shared common structure is leveraged for storage of multiple sequences through compressed encoding and neural replay, facilitating efficient information organization in working memory.
source: Together, shared common structure is leveraged for storage of multiple sequences through compressed encoding and neural replay, together facilitating efficient information organization in WM.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and neural findings

claim: Trajectory alignment manipulation differs from the Gestalt principles of perceptual organization such as proximity and similarity principles.
source: Not that the trajectory alignment manipulation differs from the Gestalt principles of perceptual organization such as proximity and similarity principles (Goldstone and Medin, 1994), and it instead reflects a higher-order relationship between maps.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction made by the authors, supported by citation to Goldstone and Medin, 1994

claim: The alignment manipulation reflects a higher-order relationship between maps.
source: Not that the trajectory alignment manipulation differs from the Gestalt principles of perceptual organization such as proximity and similarity principles (Goldstone and Medin, 1994), and it instead reflects a higher-order relationship between maps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental manipulation by the authors

claim: The alignment manipulation could not be accounted for by associative memory, since the rotational orientation for alignments between the two maps differed on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: The alignment manipulation also could not be accounted for by associative memory (Aho et al., 2022; Roads and Love, 2020), since the rotational orientation for alignments between the two maps differed on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on their experimental design, with citations to Aho et al., 2022 and Roads and Love, 2020

claim: The current study differs from recent works on structure learning and generalization because the task does not involve pre-exposure training or task-related rewards.
source: Finally, our study is also different from recent works on structure learning and generalization (Dekker et al., 2022; Garvert et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021b; Ren et al., 2022; Schapiro et al., 2013), as our task does not involve pre-exposure training or task-related rewards.
evidence: This is a distinction made by the authors, with citations to related work

claim: A congruent schema would facilitate memory retrieval compared to an incongruent condition.
source: Notably, our findings could also be understood in terms of schematic abstraction, which plays pivotal roles in memory formation (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Tse et al., 2007), such that a congruent schema would facilitate memory retrieval compared to an incongruent condition (Audrain and McAndrews, 2022; van Kesteren et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Audrain and McAndrews, 2022 and van Kesteren et al., 2010

claim: Schematic abstraction plays pivotal roles in memory formation.
source: Notably, our findings could also be understood in terms of schematic abstraction, which plays pivotal roles in memory formation (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Tse et al., 2007), such that a congruent schema would facilitate memory retrieval compared to an incongruent condition (Audrain and McAndrews, 2022; van Kesteren et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017 and Tse et al., 2007

claim: Cognitive map refers to the internal representation of spatial relations in a specific environment.
source: In fact, cognitive map refers to the internal representation of spatial relations in a specific environment (Tolman, 1948), while schematic abstraction denotes a more broad range of circumstances, whereby the gist or structure of multiple environments or episodes can be integrated (Bartlett, 1932; Farzanfar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to Tolman, 1948

claim: Schematic abstraction denotes a more broad range of circumstances, whereby the gist or structure of multiple environments or episodes can be integrated.
source: In fact, cognitive map refers to the internal representation of spatial relations in a specific environment (Tolman, 1948), while schematic abstraction denotes a more broad range of circumstances, whereby the gist or structure of multiple environments or episodes can be integrated (Bartlett, 1932; Farzanfar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to Bartlett, 1932 and Farzanfar et al., 2023

claim: Schema refers to a highly abstract framework of prior knowledge that captures common patterns across related experiences.
source: In other words, schema refers to a highly abstract framework of prior knowledge that captures common patterns across related experiences, which does not necessarily occur in a spatial framework as cognitive maps do.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge

claim: Human participants spontaneously extract underlying common structure and leverage it to organize multiple item storage without task requirement.
source: The fact that without task requirement, human participants still spontaneously extracted underlying common structure and leveraged it to organize multiple item storage reflects the intelligence of our brain to achieve efficient information coding (Attneave, 1954).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation to Attneave, 1954

claim: Participants exploit statistical regularities to form efficient working memory representation without explicit instructions to do so.
source: Indeed, there is a mountain of research suggesting that participants exploit statistical regularities to form efficient WM representation without explicit instructions to do so (e.g. Brady et al., 2009; Brady and Tenenbaum, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brady et al., 2009 and Brady and Tenenbaum, 2013

claim: Reasoning in abstract domains follows similar computational principles as in spatial domains.
source: Here, the common structure we manipulated is inspired by the theory of cognitive map (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978), which has argued that reasoning in abstract domains follows similar computational principles as in spatial domains.
evidence: Supported by citations to Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; O'keefe and Nadel, 1978

claim: There are common neural substrates for knowledge representation across domains.
source: This theory has been supported by accumulated neuroscientific evidence suggesting common neural substrates for knowledge representation across domains (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Garvert et al., 2017; Park et al., 2021; Schuck et al., 2016; Solomon et al., 2019; Theves et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple neuroscientific studies

claim: Learning process is accelerated when two different feature maps are aligned.
source: For example, learning process is accelerated when two different feature maps are aligned (Aho et al., 2022), and distance-dependent generalization is observed across two different domains in order to search for correlated rewards (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aho et al., 2022

claim: Distance-dependent generalization is observed across two different domains in order to search for correlated rewards.
source: For example, learning process is accelerated when two different feature maps are aligned (Aho et al., 2022), and distance-dependent generalization is observed across two different domains in order to search for correlated rewards (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020

claim: Neural replay was first observed in the rodent hippocampus and mainly for spatial navigation.
source: Neural replay refers to the sequential reactivation in the same or reversed order as previous experience. It was first observed in the rodent hippocampus and mainly for spatial navigation (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994), but has recently been found in many higher-level non-spatial tasks in human brains (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schapiro et al., 2018; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson and McNaughton, 1994

claim: Neural replay has recently been found in many higher-level non-spatial tasks in human brains.
source: Neural replay refers to the sequential reactivation in the same or reversed order as previous experience. It was first observed in the rodent hippocampus and mainly for spatial navigation (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994), but has recently been found in many higher-level non-spatial tasks in human brains (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021b; Schapiro et al., 2018; Schuck and Niv, 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on neural replay in humans

claim: Neural replay has been posited to represent abstract structure.
source: In fact, neural replay has been posited to represent abstract structure (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019), structure-based inference (Liu et al., 2021b), and generalization (Barry and Love, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2021 and Liu et al., 2019

claim: Neural replay has been posited to support structure-based inference.
source: In fact, neural replay has been posited to represent abstract structure (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019), structure-based inference (Liu et al., 2021b), and generalization (Barry and Love, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021b

claim: Neural replay has been posited to support generalization.
source: In fact, neural replay has been posited to represent abstract structure (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019), structure-based inference (Liu et al., 2021b), and generalization (Barry and Love, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barry and Love, 2022

claim: Color neural replay only appears for the color-location aligned sequence but not for the misaligned sequences.
source: Furthermore, color neural replay only appears for the color-location aligned sequence (AT condition) but not for the misaligned sequences (MAT condition), implicating that neural replay serves to consolidate sequences that share a common structure.
evidence: This is based on the neural decoding results comparing AT and MAT conditions

claim: Neural replay serves to consolidate sequences that share a common structure.
source: Furthermore, color neural replay only appears for the color-location aligned sequence (AT condition) but not for the misaligned sequences (MAT condition), implicating that neural replay serves to consolidate sequences that share a common structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural replay findings

claim: Structure and content are represented in a factorized manner.
source: It is posited that structure and content are represented in a factorized manner (Behrens et al., 2018; Bengio et al., 2013), and sequence structure representation that is independent of attached contents guides the replay of new experiences (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Behrens et al., 2018 and Bengio et al., 2013

claim: Sequence structure representation that is independent of attached contents guides the replay of new experiences.
